article.heading: Everything you need to know about cement

faq.q: How does this cement calculator work?
faq.a: Pick a shape (concrete slab, post hole, or a free volume), choose a mix ratio, and select the cement bag size you buy locally — 50 kg (India), 94 lb Portland (US), or a smaller retail bag. The calculator converts your job into dry volume using the standard 1.54 shrinkage factor, splits it into cement / sand / aggregate by the mix ratio, applies your wastage percentage, then rounds cement up to whole bags.

faq.q: How many bags of cement do I need for a concrete slab?
faq.a: For a typical M20 (1:1.5:3) slab, one cubic yard of concrete needs about 5 bags of 94 lb Portland cement, or roughly 8 bags of 50 kg cement. For a 10 ft × 10 ft × 4 in slab (about 1.23 cuyd) that's about 6 bags of 94 lb or 10 bags of 50 kg.

faq.q: How much cement do I need for a post hole?
faq.a: A standard 4-inch fence post in a 10-inch-wide, 24-inch-deep hole takes about 1.1 cubic feet of concrete — roughly half a 60 lb bag of pre-mix, or about 6 kg of cement plus sand for a site-mixed 1:3 fill. Enter your hole diameter, depth, and post count and the calculator returns the total.

faq.q: How much Portland cement is in a 94 lb bag?
faq.a: A 94 lb bag is the US standard for pure Portland cement and holds exactly one cubic foot of loose cement — about 42.6 kg. It's not the same as a 94 lb concrete-mix bag, which already contains sand and aggregate. If you're buying pure cement to combine with sand and aggregate on site, pick the 94 lb Portland option.

faq.q: How do I calculate cement in cubic yards?
faq.a: Multiply length × width × thickness (all in feet — convert inches by dividing by 12) to get cubic feet, then divide by 27 to get cubic yards. This calculator does the conversion for you: enter feet and inches directly and it returns cement bags for that volume.

faq.q: What mix ratio should I use — 1:2:4 or 1:1.5:3?
faq.a: 1:2:4 (M15) is fine for footpaths, patio slabs, and non-structural pours. 1:1.5:3 (M20) is the standard for house slabs, driveways, and general RCC work. 1:1:2 (M25) is used when the slab is a structural member carrying real load. For sand-and-cement work use 1:4 or 1:6.

faq.q: Does this calculator work for sand and cement only (no aggregate)?
faq.a: Yes. Pick the Brickwork mortar (1:6), Plaster mortar (1:4), or Post hole (1:3) preset — sand-and-cement mixes with zero aggregate. The output shows cement bags and sand quantity in both weight (kg) and volume (cubic feet).

faq.q: Why is the dry volume higher than the wet volume?
faq.a: When dry cement, sand, and aggregate mix into wet concrete, the fine particles fill voids in the coarser ones and the total volume shrinks. The industry-standard multiplier is 1.54 — one cubic metre of finished concrete needs about 1.54 cubic metres of loose dry ingredients before mixing.

article.heading: Everything you need to know about concrete

faq.q: How is the concrete quantity calculated?
faq.a: The wet volume you enter is multiplied by a dry-to-wet factor of 1.54 to get the loose dry volume of material needed. That dry volume is split by the mix ratio into cement, sand, and coarse aggregate, then a 3% wastage margin is added on top. Cement is converted to 50 kg bags and rounded up.

faq.q: Which mix should I pick — M15, M20, or M25?
faq.a: M20 (1:1.5:3) is the general-purpose choice for slabs, beams, and columns under light-to-moderate load. M25 (1:1:2) is the IS 456 minimum for RCC members in most structural situations. M15 and below are used for foundations, PCC, and non-structural work. Anything M30 or higher should be a design mix — not a fixed ratio like these presets.

faq.q: Why is the dry-to-wet factor 1.54?
faq.a: When dry cement, sand, and aggregate combine into wet concrete, the finer particles fill the voids in the coarser ones and the total volume shrinks. 1.54 is the industry-standard multiplier that accounts for that shrinkage — so 1 cubic metre of finished concrete needs about 1.54 cubic metres of loose dry ingredients.

faq.q: Why are my cement bags rounded up?
faq.a: Contractors buy cement in whole 50 kg bags, not fractions. The calculator rounds the cement requirement up to the next full bag so you order what's actually available. The exact kg is shown alongside if you need it for cost estimation.

faq.q: Can I change the mix ratio or wastage?
faq.a: Yes. Tick 'Customise this grade' under the preset chooser and every parameter — mix ratio, wastage percentage, cement density, bag weight, and the dry-to-wet factor — becomes editable. The preset defaults are IS 456 values for the common grades.

faq.q: Does this include steel reinforcement?
faq.a: No. Steel is calculated separately because bar schedules depend on the member type (beam, column, slab, footing) and its detailing, not on the concrete volume alone. Use the dedicated steel or rebar calculator for that.

article.heading: Everything you need to know about bricks

faq.q: How is the number of bricks calculated?
faq.a: Total masonry volume is divided by the nominal volume of a single brick — the brick plus a mortar joint on all three axes. The result is rounded up to the next whole brick, and then a wastage percentage (5% by default) is applied on top.

faq.q: What is the difference between the presets?
faq.a: Modular brick (190×90×90 mm) follows IS 1077 with a 10 mm joint — the standard used by most engineers. Traditional Indian brick (230×110×75 mm) is the common non-modular size seen widely on site. AAC block (600×200×200 mm) is a much larger, lighter unit with a thin 3 mm joint.

faq.q: How is the mortar volume calculated?
faq.a: Mortar volume = total masonry volume − volume of bricks used. That gives the wet mortar. Adding a 20% wastage factor (default) accounts for spillage and joints filling. Multiplying by a 1.33 dry-to-wet factor gives the dry cement + sand you actually need to mix.

faq.q: Why do you split cement into bags and sand into cft?
faq.a: That's how contractors and material suppliers in India quote and order — cement in 50 kg bags, sand in cubic feet. The math is done in SI internally; the answer is presented in the units you'll actually use to order.

faq.q: Can I use my own brick size and mortar ratio?
faq.a: Yes. Switch the preset dropdown to 'Custom' and every parameter — brick dimensions, joint thickness, mortar ratio, wastage percentages — becomes editable.

faq.q: Are openings subtracted correctly?
faq.a: Doors and windows are subtracted from the wall's gross area as rectangles. For arched or non-rectangular openings, approximate them with their bounding rectangle. If total openings exceed the wall area, the calculator returns an error instead of a nonsensical result.

article.heading: Everything you need to know about steel

faq.q: What's D²/162 and where does it come from?
faq.a: It's the industry shortcut for the weight per metre of a round steel bar of diameter D millimetres. It comes from π × (D/2)² × 7850 kg/cum ÷ 10⁶ ≈ D²/162.28. Contractors round to 162 in the field; use 162.28 for a slightly tighter number.

faq.q: Bar schedule vs thumb rule — which should I use?
faq.a: Bar schedule when you have the drawing and can list every bar's diameter, length, and count — the answer is accurate. Thumb rule when you're at the pricing stage and only know the concrete volume — it's rough (±20%), useful for a ballpark, not for a purchase order.

faq.q: Do the numbers include laps, bends, hooks, and chairs?
faq.a: No — Phase 1 doesn't model laps, bends, hooks, or chair bars. In bar-schedule mode, pass pre-calculated cutting lengths; in thumb-rule mode the built-in kg/cum values already absorb a rough allowance for laps. Either way, bump the wastage % if you want a bigger safety margin.

faq.q: Why do slab, beam, column, footing, and staircase all have different kg per cum?
faq.a: Denser members carry more reinforcement per unit volume. Columns and staircases are ~130 kg/cum, beams ~100, slabs ~80, footings ~70. These are Indian industry averages; override them if your consultant has a project-specific number.

article.heading: Everything you need to know about paint

faq.q: Why does my hardware store's coverage number differ from yours?
faq.a: Coverage varies a lot — brand, dilution, surface texture, and whether it's a first or re-coat all matter. Our presets are middle-of-the-road averages for the Indian market. If the paint can you're using lists its own coverage, plug that in via the Customise panel and the estimate will match exactly.

faq.q: Do I need primer under emulsion?
faq.a: For a fresh wall or one that's been putty'd, yes — primer seals the surface and stops the finish coat from soaking in unevenly. For a repaint over an existing emulsion, one coat of primer is optional if the old coat is clean and sound.

faq.q: How many finish coats should I quote for?
faq.a: Two is the industry default — one coat rarely gives even colour, especially over primer or a light-over-dark repaint. Bump to three for deep colours (dark red, navy) or high-traffic areas where you want long life.

faq.q: Why is wall putty priced by area if it's sold by weight?
faq.a: Putty is quoted at roughly 20–25 sqm per kg, so we express its coverage in the same sqm/litre style as paint to keep the calculator uniform. Treat the litre value as "units of putty" and convert to kg at purchase time using your brand's own guidance.

faq.q: Should I paint the ceiling in the same layer as the walls?
faq.a: If you're using the same finish product on both, yes — tick "include ceiling" and it's added to the net area. If ceiling paint is a different product, run two separate calculations.

article.heading: Everything you need to know about tiling

faq.q: Why is the default tile wastage 10% — higher than concrete or brick?
faq.a: Tiles waste more because cuts at walls and corners produce half-tiles that usually can't be reused. Complex layouts (diagonals, borders, small rooms) waste even more; simple square rooms with tiles that fit the module cleanly can go down to 5–7%. Adjust in Customise once you know the room.

faq.q: Thin-set adhesive vs. mortar bed — which one should I quote?
faq.a: Thin-set (tile adhesive) is the modern default — 3–5mm of cement-based adhesive, works with vitrified and ceramic tiles, sold by the bag. Mortar bed is the traditional Indian method: 20mm of cement:sand mortar laid first, then tiles pressed in. Older buildings and structural tile work still use it; new construction is almost entirely thin-set.

faq.q: Does the grout estimate include waste for spillage and mixing loss?
faq.a: No — the volume is the raw geometric fill of the joints. Real grout consumption is 15–25% higher after mixing waste, joint depth variance, and spillage. Buy at least one full bag more than the estimate suggests, especially for larger jobs.

faq.q: Do I need to include the tile thickness in the joint depth?
faq.a: Usually the grout doesn't go all the way to the substrate — it fills the top ~60–80% of the joint. We default the joint depth to the tile thickness for a conservative estimate; drop it to 6mm if you're only grouting the surface layer. Either way the volume is small and easy to over-order without much cost impact.

faq.q: How do I calculate skirting tiles or borders?
faq.a: Skirtings and borders are separate line items — they're strip pieces, cut differently, and often a different tile. Compute them separately: length of the border × height × 1.10 wastage gives the area, divide by the border-tile area to get count.

article.heading: Everything you need to know about rebar

faq.q: How much rebar do I need for a concrete slab?
faq.a: Enter the slab length and width, the centre-to-centre spacing, and the edge cover. The calculator returns the bars in each direction, the total rebar length in metres, and the number of stock bars (12 m) to order. A 6 × 4 m slab at 150 mm c/c needs roughly 66 bars and about 306 m of rebar.

faq.q: How do I calculate rebar for a slab in square feet?
faq.a: Find the slab area in square feet, divide by the spacing on each side to get the bar lines, then multiply by the bar length. The calculator does this for you and also reports rebar weight per square foot — a typical single-layer residential mesh works out to roughly 1 kg per sq ft.

faq.q: How do I calculate rebar weight?
faq.a: Rebar weight = total length × weight per metre. For diameter D in millimetres, weight per metre ≈ D² / 162 kg/m (from π × (D/2)² × 7850 kg/cum). A 12 mm bar weighs about 0.89 kg/m; a 16 mm bar about 1.58 kg/m.

faq.q: How many rebar pieces do I need for my project?
faq.a: Divide the total rebar length by the stock bar length you buy (12 m for Indian TMT) and round up. The calculator does this automatically and shows the pieces count.

faq.q: Do I need rebar in a footing or foundation?
faq.a: Almost always yes. Footings and foundations carry the full building load and need reinforcement against bending and cracking. Typical guidance: 150–200 mm c/c with 12–16 mm bars in the top and bottom meshes. Confirm against your structural drawings.

faq.q: Do I need rebar in a concrete wall?
faq.a: It depends. Retaining and foundation walls almost always need vertical rebar plus horizontal distribution bars. Simple partition walls may only need light mesh. Set the member to "wall" and confirm with an engineer.

faq.q: What is edge cover (edge-grid spacing)?
faq.a: Edge cover is the distance from the outermost rebar line to the concrete edge — the concrete around the bars that protects them from water and corrosion. The calculator subtracts two edge covers (one per end) from each dimension to get the actual grid size.

faq.q: What does rebar-per-square-metre tell me?
faq.a: It is the total rebar weight divided by the member area — a quick density check for an estimate. A single-layer 150 mm c/c 12 mm mesh is about 11–12 kg per m²; a double mesh with 16 mm bars can reach 20–25 kg per m².

article.heading: Everything you need to know about concrete volume

faq.q: How do I calculate the volume of concrete for a slab?
faq.a: Multiply length × width × depth. A 6 m × 4 m slab poured 150 mm thick is 6 × 4 × 0.15 = 3.6 cubic metres — about 4.7 cubic yards. The calculator does this in any length unit and reports cubic metres, cubic feet, and cubic yards.

faq.q: How many cubic yards of concrete do I need?
faq.a: Multiply the area by the thickness, all in the same unit, then convert to cubic yards (1 yd³ = 0.7646 m³). A 10 ft × 10 ft patio 4 inches thick is 10 × 10 × 0.333 = 33.3 ft³ ≈ 1.23 yd³ — round up to 1.3–1.5 yd³ to cover wastage.

faq.q: How much concrete do I need for a post hole?
faq.a: A post hole is a cylinder: volume = π × (diameter/2)² × depth. A 300 mm hole 600 mm deep holds about 0.042 m³ of concrete. The calculator's cylindrical mode works this out for you.

faq.q: How do I convert concrete volume between cubic metres, feet, and yards?
faq.a: 1 cubic yard = 27 cubic feet = 0.7646 cubic metres. To go the other way, 1 cubic metre = 1.308 cubic yards = 35.31 cubic feet. The calculator shows all three at once, so you never need to convert by hand.

faq.q: How much does a cubic metre of concrete weigh?
faq.a: Standard reinforced concrete weighs about 2400 kg per cubic metre (≈ 150 lb per cubic foot, ≈ 4050 lb per cubic yard). The calculator uses 2400 kg/m³ to estimate weight from the ordered volume.

faq.q: What wastage should I add when ordering concrete?
faq.a: Add 5–10% for uneven ground, over-dig, spilled mix, and formwork waste. Ready-mix suppliers quote in whole cubic yards, so a 1.23 yd³ pour usually means ordering 1.5 yd³. The calculator includes a wastage slider and applies it to the volume.

faq.q: How much concrete do I need for a footing or foundation?
faq.a: Use the same length × width × depth formula as a slab. A continuous footing is just a long rectangle — enter its length, width, and thickness. The calculator handles any unit combination and gives the volume in cubic metres, feet, and yards.

faq.q: Can I order concrete by the truck?
faq.a: Most ready-mix trucks carry 9–12 yd³. Divide your order by the truck capacity to estimate the number of loads. A 10 yd³ order fits in a single truck; larger pours need a schedule so the mix doesn't set between loads.

article.heading: Everything you need to know about concrete slabs

faq.q: How much concrete do I need for a 10×10 slab?
faq.a: A 10 ft × 10 ft slab, 4 in deep, is 33.3 ft³ — about 1.23 yd³ (0.94 m³). With 5% wastage that's roughly 1.30 yd³, about 58 bags of 80 lb premix, and about 0.2 of a 7 yd³ ready-mix truck.

faq.q: How many 80 lb bags of concrete do I need for a slab?
faq.a: One 80 lb premix bag yields about 0.6 ft³ of concrete (0.0222 yd³). Divide the slab's total volume — including wastage — by 0.0222 yd³ and round up. The calculator does this for you and also shows the 60 lb bag count.

faq.q: How do I calculate concrete yards for a slab?
faq.a: Multiply length × width × thickness, all in feet (convert inches by dividing by 12), to get cubic feet, then divide by 27 to get cubic yards. This calculator converts any mix of units for you and reports cubic metres too.

faq.q: How thick should a concrete slab be?
faq.a: 100–125 mm (4–5 in) suits paths, patios, and shed floors; 150 mm (6 in) is standard for driveways and garage floors. Heavier vehicle loads need a thicker slab or reinforcement — confirm with a structural engineer.

faq.q: How much does a concrete slab weigh?
faq.a: A 6 m × 4 m slab, 150 mm thick, is 3.6 m³ of concrete. At 2400 kg/m³ that's about 8640 kg (8.64 tonnes). The calculator shows the estimated weight of your ordered volume.

faq.q: How many ready-mix trucks do I need?
faq.a: A standard ready-mix truck carries about 7 yd³. Divide your ordered volume by 7 to get the number of loads. A 6 m × 4 m slab at 150 mm is roughly 4.7 yd³ — most of a single load.

faq.q: How much wastage should I add for a concrete slab?
faq.a: Add 5–10% for an uneven subgrade, spilled mix, and formwork waste. The default of 5% suits a flat prepared site; use 10% for rough ground or when ordering by the bag.
